evals.prompt: I maintain Quillrope, a Rust crate for streaming CSV parsing. About 41,000 crates depend on it directly or transitively, we get roughly 120 issues a month, and there are three of us with merge rights: me, Dara and Sasha. Almost nobody sends patches. Last year we had 9 external contributors and 6 of them sent a single typo fix. I've been reading Python's PEP 13 and the Kubernetes election docs and I want to set up a five-seat steering council with two-year staggered terms and an election officer, in place before the 2.0 release in March. Can you draft the structure?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to install the requested elected body, a diagnosis of the project as a many-users/few-contributors shape, two ranked models with monthly hours and reversibility, a maintainer council recommended, and succession plus scope defence named as the real work.
expectations: Classifies the project as the 'stadium' shape (many users, very few contributors) using the two-axis Working in Public / Eghbal taxonomy, named rather than presented as a generic observation.
States that for this shape the scarce resource is maintainer attention, and names curation, scope defence and succession as the actual work.
Does not deliver the requested five-seat elected steering committee as the recommendation.
States that an elected steering committee carries the highest value and the highest effort, and therefore loses on the value-per-maintainer-hour ordering.
Recommends a maintainer council, naming it the default at three or more maintainers.
Presents exactly two models with trade-offs plus one recommendation, rather than a single option or a long menu.
Attaches a monthly effort figure to each presented model, next to what those hours buy.
States how easily each presented model can be reversed or undone.

Names at least one of the four conditions that would promote an elected steering committee anyway (maintainers on more than one payroll, a visible founder departure, a contributor base outgrowing the maintainer set, a foundation application with a stated governance bar) and states that none of them holds here.
States that the March 2.0 date favours models that install in an afternoon and works against an elected body, because an election's legitimacy cannot be compressed.
Produces an as-is statement of who decides today, and by what implicit rule, before proposing any model.
Computes or asks for the contributor absence factor before ranking shared models.
Warns that a governance document describing elections the project never holds reads as theatre to contributors and is treated as a defect by reviewers.

evals.prompt: Numbers for Halyard, our open-source feature-flag SDK, over the last 12 months straight out of git shortlog -sn: renovate[bot] 1240, Priya 980, Tomas 430, Ines 350, Karl 310, Wen 190, then four people at 60, 40, 30 and 20. Priya runs the merge queue, so 610 of her 980 are merge commits. Karl is the only person who has touched the Windows backend in two years. Priya holds the npm token and the release signing key and nobody else does. Our board deck says our bus factor is 4. Is that right?
evals.expected_output: A recomputed contributor absence factor with bots and merge commits stripped out, per-area figures, a separate credential inventory, and the correction of the claimed number.
expectations: Uses the term 'contributor absence factor' and attributes the metric definition to CHAOSS, or notes it was formerly called bus factor.
States the definition as the smallest number of contributors responsible for 50% of contributions.
Excludes the bot author from the calculation and says why.
Excludes Priya's 610 merge commits and says why, namely that the integrator otherwise looks like the author.
Reports a corrected project-wide absence factor of 3.
Rejects the claimed figure of 4.
Shows the arithmetic: the corrected total, the 50% threshold, and the accumulation that crosses it.
States that the factor must be computed per governed area as well as project-wide.
Reports the Windows backend as an area with an absence factor of 1, and names a single-owner subsystem as what actually breaks on a departure.
States that the measure should also run on reviews, issue responses and documentation, not commits alone.
Produces a separate inventory of privileged credentials rather than treating code access as the binding constraint.
Flags Priya alone holding the npm token and the signing key as a single point of failure, and calls for two current holders on every credential row.
Labels the 'at least 2, and two holders per credential' figure as a self-set baseline rather than a published standard.
Warns against publishing per-person contribution league tables and recommends reporting aggregates.

evals.prompt: I'm the only maintainer of Brightsea, a Python library for parsing scientific instrument files. Around 900 projects depend on it. I've done this alone for six years and I'm cooked: no release in five months, 340 open issues. Someone going by 'ferrous_owl' showed up seven months ago, has 34 merged PRs, is unbelievably responsive, and has offered to take over releases entirely. They've asked twice this week for PyPI publish rights and the GPG key so they can ship 4.0 before the SciPy conference. Honestly I want to hand them everything and walk away. What do I do?
evals.expected_output: Load relief first, merge rights granted quickly, keys withheld behind a supervised release cycle, and the urgency treated as a signal to slow down.
expectations: States that promotion is not a treatment for burnout, and that load relief comes first.
Names concrete relief moves before any grant: triage help, scope cuts, funding, or pausing releases.
Separates merge and review rights from privileged credentials as two distinct grants.
Recommends granting merge rights quickly, on the grounds that they are cheap to grant and cheap to revoke.
Withholds PyPI publish rights and the signing key until at least one supervised release cycle has happened.
States that key-holder rights are never granted in the same act as merge rights.
Treats the repeated urgency and the conference deadline as a reason to slow down rather than to accelerate.
States that a legitimate co-maintainer can wait a release cycle.
References the 2024 xz-utils takeover (or CVE-2024-3094), including the multi-year credibility build and the pressure applied to an exhausted solo maintainer.

Presents the conflict between the liberal-commit-access position attributed to @felixge via opensource.guide and the post-xz staged-grant position, and resolves it as generous with the ladder, slow with the keys, rather than silently picking one side.
Says the governance document should state that the staging pause is policy rather than distrust.
Recommends a second key holder rather than transferring sole custody from one person to another.
Recommends counting reviews given, not only pull requests merged, as promotion evidence.
For key-holder roles, prefers a verifiable identity or an established public track record, and says the requirement belongs in the document rather than being applied silently.

evals.prompt: Context: Vantablock is our stream-processing engine, Apache-2.0 since day one, built at Corvid Systems where I run the platform team. Marketing wants to publish 'Vantablock is now a vendor-neutral open project' next month ahead of our user conference. Current state: five maintainers, all Corvid employees; the trademark and vantablock.io are registered to Corvid; we require a CLA that assigns us broad rights; we run a maintainers' sync every Tuesday, internal, no minutes. Two large banks are evaluating us and one has asked procurement to check governance. Can you help me write the announcement?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to announce first, the four neutrality signals audited with a verdict each, and the ordered sequence a real move to neutrality has to follow.
expectations: Declines to lead with the announcement, stating that neutrality is transferred rather than announced.
Runs the four checkable signals in order of weight: trademark, domains and registry accounts; maintainer-affiliation ratio; contribution-agreement shape; published minutes.
Returns a per-signal verdict rather than prose impressions.
States that the Apache-2.0 licence passes the licence row and fixes nothing on the other four.
States explicitly that code-license openness and governance openness are two separate audits.
Reports the five-of-five single-employer maintainer ratio as the signal that classifies the project as single-vendor.
Cites the pre-fork Redis position, where only two of five maintainers worked outside the controlling company, as a case where the affiliation ratio preceded a fork.
Gives the sequence in the right order: maintainers from a second organization first, then vote or seat caps, then the trademark and asset transfer.
States that announcing before the maintainer pool changes reads as marketing and is checked as marketing.
Cites the Istio trademark episode and the read that partners judge where the asset landed, not the sincerity of the arrangement.
States that a company CLA with a broad grant is what makes a later unilateral relicense possible, and names it as the lever procurement will look for.
Routes the trademark transfer and the contribution agreement to legal counsel instead of advising on their terms.
Recommends published, versioned minutes on a real cadence, with private categories enumerated and a visible marker left where content was withheld.

evals.prompt: We're submitting Kerrigold Mesh to a foundation's sandbox intake in about six weeks. Four maintainers, all at Northgate Labs, no governance file at all right now. I've drafted a GOVERNANCE.md with a five-seat technical steering committee, staggered two-year terms, an appointed election officer, a contribution-based electorate and three working groups (security, docs, release). Can you review it and tighten the language before we submit?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to polish the over-engineered draft, the smaller honest model recommended with a revisit trigger, and the readiness gaps listed in fix order with the slow ones called out.
expectations: Declines to tighten the drafted structure as-is, and names it as over-engineered for four maintainers at a single employer.
States that governance documented but never exercised is a review-blocking defect, not a neutral omission.
Names adopting a complex structure shortly before a foundation application as a recognized anti-pattern.
Names the concrete costs of the draft: elections that never happen, expired terms, working groups with one member, and a reviewer distrusting the whole document because one part is false.
Recommends writing the smaller, honest model instead, and recording a revisit trigger such as maintainers exceeding eight or a second organization holding two seats.
Identifies the single-employer maintainer pool as one of the two slow readiness gaps that take quarters rather than days.
Identifies governance never exercised as the other slow gap.

Lists the remaining readiness gaps in fix order: repository permissions contradicting documented roles, unclear ownership of the name, domains or registry accounts, missing community-health files or a stale maintainers list, and no adopters willing to be named publicly.
States that what a graduation gate certifies is that no single company can walk away and kill the project, rather than code quality.
Quotes any foundation threshold with the foundation named as its owner, rather than as a generic standard.
Marks which requirements are legal gates for counsel (IP clearance, software grant, trademark, membership or sponsorship agreement) rather than ranking them alongside choices.
Advises confirming the target foundation's published criteria as currently stated rather than relying on remembered figures.
Recommends producing evidence that the rules have actually run at least once, such as a maintainer added or moved to emeritus, a vote held, or an escalation resolved under the written path.

evals.prompt: Quick one. I'm writing the decision-making section of our GOVERNANCE.md for Tinpot, a small Go HTTP router with 4 maintainers spread across Lisbon, Bangalore and Vancouver. What are the industry-standard numbers for: the comment period before a breaking change, the threshold to remove a maintainer, how long before someone counts as inactive, and how many approvals to merge? Just give me the standard values so I can paste them in.
evals.expected_output: Every figure quoted with its owning project attached, published values separated from self-set baselines, and a warning against pasting any of them unchanged.
expectations: Declines to present any figure as an industry standard, stating that the field has conventions rather than standards.
Attributes every quoted figure to its owning project or body, in the shape 'Node.js waits 72 hours' rather than 'the standard is 72 hours'.
Quotes the pattern of two approvals to land a change, dropping to one once the change has sat 7 days, attributed to Node.js.
Quotes a minimum 72-hour voting period with its stated reason of letting other time zones take part, attributed to Apache.
Quotes a final comment period of 10 days with a minimum of 5 business days, attributed to the Rust RFC process.
Labels the two-thirds removal and amendment threshold as a common template value with a named source, not as a standard.
Labels the 6-to-12-month inactivity definition as a common convention rather than a standard.
Separates published figures from self-set baselines explicitly, and says which of its own recommendations are which.
Recommends the aging-approval rule as the single most useful import for a small maintainer team, because it stops the repository stalling when one maintainer is away.
Advises adjusting every window for community size and timezone spread rather than pasting the numbers unchanged.
Warns that a named project's published thresholds change, and that the project's own governance file should be re-checked before the number is quoted.
Notes that a team split across three widely separated timezones changes whether a given voting window actually buys the participation it was meant to buy.

evals.prompt: Rough month. Marrowfen, our self-hosted photo library, had a blow-up: our moderation lead resigned publicly after a thread about a corporate sponsor, two other maintainers quit in solidarity, and there are now three competing Matrix rooms arguing about it. People keep saying we need 'real governance'. I want to run a constitutional assembly, elect a steering committee in December, and publish a full governance charter to settle this. Where do I start?
evals.expected_output: A recommendation to repair the conflict before publishing any structure, the conduct dimension routed out of the governance ladder, and concentration recomputed after the departures.
expectations: States that writing new governance during a live trust conflict relocates the fight rather than settling it.
Cites the precedent of a major project that produced an elected steering committee and two forks in the same year.
Recommends addressing the conflict first and publishing the structure afterwards, in that order.
Declines to schedule the December election as the opening move.
Routes the conduct dimension to the code-of-conduct process rather than through the governance escalation ladder.
States that conduct cases are handled in private, with the accused excluded from deliberation.
Specifies that where a maintainer is the subject, others handle it, escalating outside the project if the whole group is implicated.
Names recusal for anyone employed by a party to the dispute, with a named fallback for when recusal leaves no quorum.
Warns that the resignations have probably moved the contributor absence factor, and calls for recomputing concentration and credential holders now.
Treats the sponsorship dimension as a money-governance question (conflict-of-interest policy, who authorizes spending) distinct from the choice of governance model.
Does not present an elected steering committee as the remedy for the trust conflict.
Advises that when structure is eventually published, the simplest workable ladder is what sticks, not the most sophisticated one.

evals.prompt: Here is the entire decision section of our GOVERNANCE.md for Pallasite, an embedded database with two maintainers, me and Jonas: 'Significant changes are discussed by the community until consensus is reached. The maintainers will consider all feedback and make the best decision for the project. Maintainers are added when the existing maintainers feel someone is ready.' A contributor opened an issue last week saying this is meaningless. Jonas thinks it's fine. Who's right?
evals.expected_output: The contributor's objection upheld with specific defects named, a bounded and escalatable rewrite, self-assessable promotion criteria, and the missing decision classes enumerated.
expectations: Sides with the contributor and names the specific defects: 'significant' undefined, 'consensus' with no test, no clock, and nobody named as decider.
States that a rule that cannot be violated cannot be relied on.
Rewrites the clause into a bounded, testable, escalatable form carrying a named decider, a threshold, a stated window and an escalation path.
Names a specific escalation body or tiebreaker, since a two-person project cannot reach a majority.
Requires any blocking objection to carry a technical justification, so that a veto is an argument rather than a mood.
Puts a timer on every decision path, naming the unbounded thread as the failure mode of consensus-seeking.
States what happens when the timer expires: the proposal is explicitly declined or held, or defaults to the status quo, rather than the issue staying open forever.
Replaces the promotion sentence with self-assessable criteria combining a time period, a count of non-trivial merged contributions, and a count of substantive reviews.
Explains that the original promotion wording leaves a contributor nothing to act on, so nobody applies and the maintainer pool never grows.
Enumerates the decision classes the section is missing, at minimum routine change, breaking change, new maintainer, removal, scope change, release, security response and amendment.
Specifies quorum, minimum open period, and whether abstentions count in the denominator for any vote it defines.
Names lazy consensus as the default for routine work, and excludes it from irreversible actions such as a release, a key rotation or a removal.
Labels any threshold it proposes as a self-set baseline the project may move, rather than as a standard.

evals.prompt: Two of us run Sandglass, a date-formatting library with roughly 6,000 weekly downloads. My co-maintainer Nadia goes on parental leave for five months starting in January, and I travel for work a lot. We've never had a governance file. I want one page that actually helps us, not a constitution. What goes in it and what do we leave out?
evals.expected_output: A roughly one-page GOVERNANCE.md in the standard section order, every clause passing the has-done-or-will-plausibly-do test, with the absence, emeritus and end-state clauses carrying the value.
expectations: Produces a GOVERNANCE.md of roughly one page rather than a multi-section constitution.
Applies the clause test explicitly: every clause must describe something the project has done or will plausibly do this year.
Follows the template section order for the sections it keeps, and skips the ones the project does not need rather than reordering.
Lists merge rights separately from privileged credentials such as signing, publishing and organization ownership in the roles section.
Includes an aging-approval or single-approver rule so that routine changes can still land while one of the two maintainers is away.
Includes a scope sentence stating what the project refuses to become, so that features can be declined impersonally.
Includes an inactivity definition in months and an emeritus clause with rights removed, credit retained, and reinstatement stated.
Includes a named end state: a successor named, or an archive announced publicly, rather than the project going silent.
States that an archive announcement marks the repository read-only, states the last supported version and the security policy, and points at a successor fork if one exists.
Says explicitly that the project holds no meetings, rather than inventing a meeting cadence.
Links the neighbouring files (contribution mechanics, code of conduct, people file, security policy) rather than absorbing their content, so that a process tweak is not a governance amendment.
Includes an amendments clause with a threshold and a window, plus a line stating that changing the document is expected rather than a crisis.
Recommends publishing the reduced-availability period, and treats a stated weekly time budget as a legitimate governance clause rather than something to keep quiet about.

evals.prompt: Thornfield is a monorepo: core runtime, CLI, web dashboard, Terraform provider, Helm charts and a VS Code extension. Six top-level directories, six maintainers. Everything is slow because every change seems to need everyone's attention. I want to split it into six subprojects, each with its own SIG, its own charter and its own maintainer list, with a small top-level council above them, like Kubernetes does. Here's the thing though: all six of us work across all six directories, we have maybe four regular outside contributors total, and nobody has more than about two hours a week for process. Plan it out?
evals.expected_output: Federation ruled out by gate rather than ranked low, delegation and review rules offered as the real fix for throughput, and a maintainer council recommended.
expectations: Rules federated subprojects out rather than ranking it low or parking it at the bottom of a menu.
Names the gate that rules it out: components without their own contributor communities make federation unadoptable.
Says explicitly that the model was deleted from consideration and why, rather than leaving it listed.
States that the stated effort ceiling of roughly two hours a week each independently removes federation from consideration.
States that federation buys cross-component deadlock resolution and little else, which is not the problem described.
Notes that federation is wrong as a starting point because it multiplies process before there is anyone to govern.
Names the real cost shape: roughly a week per charter, then a standing job for each subproject, with diverged cadences resisting re-merging.
Recommends delegation, meaning named per-area owners or working groups with a written scope and a report-back expectation, as the cheaper answer to the review bottleneck.
Recommends a maintainer council as the model that fits six maintainers working in one shared area.
States that if federation is ever pursued, the first subproject is chartered as an experiment with explicit scope and a review date.
Gives the premature-split test: if the council still makes all of the subprojects' decisions, the split was premature.
Distinguishes the review-throughput complaint from a governance-model problem, and addresses throughput with approval and review rules rather than a structural change.

evals.prompt: Cinderpath, our infrastructure testing tool, is BUSL-1.1 licensed. A fintech wants to sponsor us at $48,000 a year and a European bank wants to pay for two features. Right now the money would land in my personal bank account, which my accountant hates. I've been told to apply to Software Freedom Conservancy. I also read somewhere that 15-20% of sandbox projects get archived within three years, so I want to factor that risk in. Three maintainers, two of us at the same consultancy. What's the path?
evals.expected_output: The named sponsor ruled out on its licence requirement, the unverified archival statistic refused as a planning input, host types distinguished, and the money-governance components specified.
expectations: Reports that the named fiscal sponsor requires a licence that is both OSI-approved and DFSG-free, and that BUSL-1.1 does not meet it, so that route is closed as things stand.
Refuses to use the 15-20% archival figure as a planning input, and states that it is unverified against any foundation's own data.

Distinguishes lightweight fiscal hosting (donation handling, no governance imposed, a percentage of donations) from a fiscal sponsor with legal services (around 10% of processed revenue, written decision-making required, asset assignment optional).
States that a fiscal host removes the need to incorporate, and that a legal entity is unnecessary until money is involved.
Runs the join-or-not test on all three axes: money, neutrality, and the autonomy budget.

Names the money-governance components required once funds exist: a written conflict-of-interest policy, a budget approved by the governing body rather than by whoever holds the payment credentials, spending-authorization thresholds, a reserve target, and a transparency mechanism.
Names paid maintainers as the recurring friction once some contributors draw project funds and others do not.
Recommends funding a defined administrative or triage role rather than feature development, separating paying for upkeep from paying to decide direction.
Flags the two-of-three same-employer maintainer ratio as a neutrality signal the sponsor and the bank will read.

Tells the user to confirm which legal entity actually holds the funds, and to write the exit plan while nothing is wrong, citing the 2024 staged dissolution of a charitable fiscal host that affected more than 600 collectives with roughly seven months to spend down or transfer.
Notes that a fiscal sponsor holding assigned assets typically cannot later transfer them to an individual or a for-profit, and that the irreversibility is what an adopter reads.
Routes any licence change, the sponsorship or membership agreement, and contributor agreements to legal counsel rather than advising on their terms.
Warns that a US charitable-status application is not a formality, citing a denial that arrived after roughly four and a half years.

evals.prompt: Our GOVERNANCE.md for Ravenbrook, an observability agent, says: four maintainers (Ash, Bo, Colm, Dee), three area owners for collector, exporters and docs, and that 'release authority rests with the maintainer group'. Reality check I just ran on the org: nine accounts have admin on the repo, including two people who left the company in 2025; branch protection is off on main; CODEOWNERS routes everything to @ravenbrook/core, which contains Ash and someone who hasn't committed in 19 months; and only Bo can publish to the registry. A prospective customer's open-source office is doing a review next month. The doc reads fine, so what else should we do?
evals.expected_output: A line-by-line diff of the repository and organization settings against the document, with divergence named as the review-blocking finding and each contradiction assigned a fix.
expectations: States that documented roles contradicted by repository permissions is a named review-blocking anti-pattern that reviewers check for.
Rejects the premise that the document reading fine is sufficient.
Produces a diff of the actual repository and organization settings against the document, item by item.
Flags the nine admin accounts, including the two departed people, as the roles-versus-permissions contradiction to fix first.
Treats a departed person retaining access as a security matter rather than a tidiness matter.
Flags branch protection being off as contradicting any documented review requirement.
States that code-owner routing must match both the areas named in governance and who actually touches them in the commit history, and calls this a computable diff rather than an opinion.
Flags the 19-month-inactive code owner and ties it to a written inactivity definition and an emeritus path.
Flags Bo as the sole registry publisher, and requires more than one holder for registry publishing, release signing and organization ownership.
Requires a people file listing current affiliations plus a separate emeritus section.
States that zero contradictions between documented roles and repository permissions is binary and not a threshold the project can adjust downward.
States that where the forge exposes no setting for a documented rule, the manual convention replacing it must be written down.

evals.prompt: Sablewire is our workflow engine. I'm VP Engineering at Kestrel Data, where it started. Two companies that use it heavily, Munro Freight and Alto Health, have each put an engineer on it full time, so we're now seven maintainers: five Kestrel, two external. Kestrel sells a hosted Sablewire Cloud, owns the trademark, and honestly we do need to control when releases go out because our cloud rollouts are tied to them. Our roadmap is still decided in a Kestrel planning meeting. The two new maintainers are great but I can tell they're wary. Draft us something.
evals.expected_output: Reserved rights stated in writing, per-organization caps adopted now while uncontroversial, the roadmap moved into public issues, and asset separation flagged as urgent.
expectations: States that more than one company now employing maintainers makes asset separation urgent now, while moving the trademark and domains is still uncontroversial.
Writes out explicitly what the company reserves - brand, hosted product, release timing - as a stated clause rather than leaving it implicit.
States that what triggers a maintainer revolt is an assurance that drifts, not a limit that was stated up front.
Recommends per-organization seat or vote caps, and says to adopt them while the seat count is still small enough for the cap to be uncontroversial.
Describes organization-balanced voting correctly: one vote per employer, independents counting as their own, applied to listed decision types, while day-to-day merges stay on lazy consensus.
Moves roadmap decisions out of the internal planning meeting and into public issues.
Names invisible control - an internal roadmap meeting, a trademark on a company balance sheet, one shared employer - as the specific risk of a company-backed project.
Adds that maintainer nominations are judged without prejudice to employer, plus a cap on nominations from an organization already employing half the maintainers.
Reports the five-of-seven affiliation ratio as still classifying the project as single-vendor by the measure adopters and researchers use.
Cites the .NET Foundation episode, or its read that creating a foundation does not by itself remove the founder's authority: only the asset transfer and the bylaw amendment rule do.
Names 'maintainers on more than one payroll' as one of the conditions that promotes an elected steering committee, and states that it is now met.
Routes the trademark arrangement and any contributor agreement to legal counsel rather than drafting terms.
Recommends published, versioned minutes on a real cadence, with the categories that may be decided privately enumerated.
